newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey gets bids for second phase of Iran gas line.
newsitem.headline: Turkey gets bids for second phase of Iran gas line.

text.p: Turkey collected bids on Wednesday for the construction of the second phase of a pipeline that will eventually carry gas from Iran's Tabriz to the Turkish capital Ankara under a $23 billion agreement, officials said.

The second phase of the pipeline, which will be 1,420 km (888 miles) long in total and carry up to 10 billion cubic metres annually, will be laid in two sections -- one from Erzurum in eastern Turkey to Sivas and from Sivas to Ankara.

Epsilon-AGE, a Turkish consortium, offered the lowest bid of $43.1 million to build the first section of 450 km (281 miles) from Erzurum to Sivas among the nine participating consortia in the publicly-held tender, officials from Botas, state pipeline company, said.

Kalyon Insaat-Kalyon Yapi, another Turkish consortium, gave the lowest bid of $37.8 million for the second section from Sivas to Ankara which will be 465 km (291 miles) long. Botas said it received 12 bids for the second section.
"The assessments will take about a month then contracts will be signed with the winners," said one official from Botas, which carried out the tender.
Among the participating companies were French Sofregas, SAE, Italy's Saipem, Russia's Stroytransgas and Rosneftegastroi.

The entire pipeline's 300-km (188-mile) first phase from the Iranian border to Erzurum was awarded to a Turkish consortium, which will provide for the pipes, for $117.5 million and the construction work was started in May.
Unlike the first phase, Botas will be supplying pipes for the second phase of the line.
Iran has begun building a pipeline from Tabriz to the Turkish border.

The pipeline will carry an annual three bcm of initially Turkmen gas from Tabriz to Erzurum from 1998, according to the gas and pipeline agreement. The amount will be raised to 10 bcm by 2005, including Iranian gas supplies.

The Turkey-Iran gas agreement, signed last August, drew criticism from Ankara's chief ally Washington, which told Turkey to look to other gas suppliers than Iran, which, along with Libya, it accused of supporting "terrorism" and vowed to punish companies investing more than $40 million in both countries.
Turkey has said the pipeline deal does not breach the U.S. restriction, citing Iran and Turkey were building the pipeline in their own territories by themselves.
